notes: BATCH_008, Quantitative Aptitude part: 199 original questions (60 Basic, 79 Intermediate, 60 Advanced) with 10 shared DI stimuli on new data sets. Every answer was recomputed by tools/batch_008/quant.py before writing; every number series was also tested against a library of common alternative rules (no other rule that fits the given terms produces another option); quantity-comparison values are at least 2% apart. Questions tagged ai:independent-check were also re-solved from the stem, options and data set alone by a separate solver. Pending human review.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If 2^(x + y) = 64 and 3^(x − y) = 1/9, what is the value of 2x + y?

solution.concept: Write both right sides as powers of the same base and compare exponents: 64 = 2⁶ and 1/9 = 3⁻²
solution.explanation: 2^(x + y) = 2⁶ gives x + y = 6. 3^(x − y) = 3⁻² gives x − y = −2. Adding, 2x = 4, so x = 2 and y = 4. Then 2x + y = 4 + 4 = 8.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 drops the minus sign (x − y = 2 gives x = 4, y = 2); 6 is x + y, not 2x + y; 8.5 writes 1/9 as 3⁻¹ (x − y = −1 gives x = 2.5, y = 3.5).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
√6,889 − ∛19,683 = ?

solution.concept: Unit-digit method: a square ending in 9 has a root ending in 3 or 7; a cube ending in 3 has a cube root ending in 7
solution.explanation: 6,889 lies between 80² = 6,400 and 90² = 8,100 and ends in 9, so its root is 83 or 87; 83² = 6,889. 19,683 lies between 20³ and 30³ and ends in 3, so its cube root ends in 7: 27³ = 19,683. 83 − 27 = 56.
solution.shortcut: For the square root, 85² = 7,225 > 6,889, so the root is below 85: 83, not 87.
solution.why_others_wrong: 60 picks 87 as the square root (87² = 7,569); 46 takes the cube root as 37; 110 adds the two roots.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If 4ᵃ = 5 and 5ᵇ = 32, what is the value of ab?

solution.concept: Substitute one equation into the other: (4ᵃ)ᵇ = 4^(ab)
solution.explanation: 5ᵇ = 32 and 5 = 4ᵃ, so (4ᵃ)ᵇ = 32, i.e. 4^(ab) = 32. Writing both as powers of 2: 2^(2ab) = 2⁵, so 2ab = 5 and ab = 5/2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 treats 4^(ab) as 2^(ab), forgetting that 4 = 2²; 8 divides 32 by 4 as if the exponents were factors; 2/5 inverts the result (it is the value of 1/(ab)).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y that holds for every pair of roots.
I. x² − 20x + 99 = 0
II. y² − 25y + 156 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise: find two numbers with the given sum and product
solution.explanation: I: 9 + 11 = 20 and 9 × 11 = 99, so x = 9 or 11. II: 12 + 13 = 25 and 12 × 13 = 156, so y = 12 or 13. The largest x (11) is below the smallest y (12), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y reverse the comparison: every root of I is smaller than every root of II.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the roots of I and II and decide how x is related to y.
I. x² + 4x − 45 = 0
II. y² − 10y + 25 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Equation II is a perfect square, so it has one repeated root
solution.explanation: I: (x + 9)(x − 5) = 0, so x = 5 or −9. II: (y − 5)² = 0, so y = 5 only. x = 5 equals y and x = −9 is less than y, so x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for x = 5 = y; x ≥ y fails for x = −9.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve the two equations and choose the relation between x and y, if any, that holds for all their roots.
I. 3x² − 8x − 35 = 0
II. 2y² − 13y + 21 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Split the middle term: −8x = −15x + 7x and −13y = −7y − 6y
solution.explanation: I: 3x² − 15x + 7x − 35 = (3x + 7)(x − 5) = 0, so x = 5 or −7/3. II: 2y² − 7y − 6y + 21 = (2y − 7)(y − 3) = 0, so y = 3.5 or 3. x = 5 is greater than both values of y, but x = −2.33 is smaller than both, so no single relation holds.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y fail for x = −7/3 (a sign slip that reads the root as +7/3 makes them look true); x ≤ y and x < y fail for x = 5.
solution.final_answer: Option D: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I is linear and equation II is quadratic. Solve both and choose the relation between x and y.
I. 5(x − 2) = 2(x + 7)
II. y² − 17y + 72 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Solve the linear equation fully before comparing; a shared value makes the relation non-strict
solution.explanation: I: 5x − 10 = 2x + 14, so 3x = 24 and x = 8. II: (y − 8)(y − 9) = 0, so y = 8 or 9. x = 8 equals one root and is less than the other, so x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y overlooks that x = 8 equals the root y = 8; x > y reverses the comparison of 8 with 9.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve the linear equation I and the quadratic equation II and state the relation between x and y.
I. x/3 + x/5 = 16
II. y² − 51y + 650 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Clear the fractions in I with the LCM 15
solution.explanation: I: (5x + 3x)/15 = 16, so 8x = 240 and x = 30. II: 25 + 26 = 51 and 25 × 26 = 650, so y = 25 or 26. x = 30 is greater than both, so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y come from clearing the fractions wrongly: 8x = 16 (forgetting to multiply 16 by 15) gives x = 2, below both roots of II.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I contains √x (the non-negative square root of x). Find every x and y and choose the relation between them.
I. x − 7√x + 12 = 0
II. y² − 33y + 272 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Treat I as a quadratic in √x: (√x)² − 7√x + 12 = 0
solution.explanation: I: (√x − 3)(√x − 4) = 0, so √x = 3 or 4 and x = 9 or 16. II: 16 + 17 = 33 and 16 × 17 = 272, so y = 16 or 17. x = 16 equals y = 16 and every other pair has x < y. So x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y misses the shared value 16 (it also follows from stopping at √x = 3, 4 without squaring); x ≥ y fails for x = 9.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I is a cubic. Find all its real roots and the roots of II, then choose the relation between x and y.
I. x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 = 0
II. y² − 9y + 20 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Try small integers: x = 1 makes the cubic zero, so (x − 1) is a factor
solution.explanation: x = 1 gives 1 − 6 + 11 − 6 = 0, so x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 = (x − 1)(x² − 5x + 6) = (x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 3). So x = 1, 2 or 3. II: (y − 4)(y − 5) = 0, so y = 4 or 5. The largest x (3) is below the smallest y (4), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y reverse the comparison: even the largest root of I (3) is below the smallest root of II (4).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I has an irrational coefficient (√2 ≈ 1.414). Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y, if any, that holds for all roots.
I. x² + 2√2x − 6 = 0
II. y² − 2y − 3 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Look for factors of the form (x + a√2)(x − b√2) with ab × 2 = 6 and (a − b)√2 = 2√2
solution.explanation: I: (x + 3√2)(x − √2) = 0, since 3√2 × √2 = 6 and 3√2 − √2 = 2√2. So x = √2 ≈ 1.41 or −3√2 ≈ −4.24. II: (y − 3)(y + 1) = 0, so y = 3 or −1. x = 1.41 is less than 3 but greater than −1, so no relation holds.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for x = 1.41, y = −1; x ≥ y fails for x = −4.24; x > y and x ≤ y fail for the same pairs.
solution.final_answer: Option C: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the least number that must be added to 7,385 so that the sum is exactly divisible by 12?

solution.concept: Find the remainder on division by 12; the number to add is 12 minus that remainder
solution.explanation: 12 × 615 = 7,380, so 7,385 leaves a remainder of 5. Adding 12 − 5 = 7 gives 7,392 = 12 × 616.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 is the remainder, which would have to be subtracted, not added; 3 makes 7,388, divisible by 4 but not by 3 (digit sum 26); 1 makes 7,386, divisible by 3 but not by 4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the greatest number that divides 398, 436 and 542 leaving remainders 7, 11 and 15 respectively?

solution.concept: Subtract each remainder first; the required number is the HCF of the results
solution.why_others_wrong: 34 = 2 × 17 does not divide the odd number 425; 51 = 3 × 17 does not divide 425 (digit sum 11); 23 divides 391 but not 425 or 527.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the remainder when 1! + 2! + 3! + … + 100! is divided by 12?

solution.concept: From 4! = 24 onwards every factorial is a multiple of 12, so only the first three terms matter
solution.explanation: 4! = 24 and every later factorial contains 24 as a factor, so each leaves remainder 0. The remainder therefore comes from 1! + 2! + 3! = 1 + 2 + 6 = 9.
steps: n! is a multiple of 12 for n ≥ 4
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 assumes every term is a multiple of 12; 3 also drops 3! = 6, which is not a multiple of 12; 1 keeps only 1!.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the unit digit of 1¹ + 2² + 3³ + 4⁴ + … + 10¹⁰?

solution.concept: Find the unit digit of each term from the cycle of its last digit, then add the unit digits
solution.explanation: Unit digits: 1¹ → 1, 2² → 4, 3³ → 7, 4⁴ → 6, 5⁵ → 5, 6⁶ → 6, 7⁷ → 3 (cycle 7, 9, 3, 1; 7 mod 4 = 3), 8⁸ → 6 (cycle 8, 4, 2, 6; 8 mod 4 = 0), 9⁹ → 9, 10¹⁰ → 0. Sum = 47, so the unit digit is 7.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 takes the unit digit of 7⁷ as 7 (sum 51); 9 takes the unit digit of 8⁸ as 8 (sum 49); 5 adds the bases 1 + 2 + … + 10 = 55, ignoring the powers.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the largest number that divides n⁵ − n exactly for every natural number n?

solution.concept: Factorise n⁵ − n = (n − 1)n(n + 1)(n² + 1) and test the smallest case n = 2
solution.explanation: (n − 1)n(n + 1) is a product of three consecutive integers, so it is divisible by 6. By Fermat's little theorem, n⁵ − n is also divisible by 5. So 30 always divides it. For n = 2, n⁵ − n = 30, so no number larger than 30 can always divide it.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 and 6 always divide n⁵ − n but are not the largest such number; 60 fails for n = 2, where n⁵ − n = 30.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: When a number is increased by 15%, it becomes 391. What is the number?

solution.concept: After a 15% increase the number is 115% of the original, so divide by 1.15
solution.why_others_wrong: 332.35 takes 15% off 391 (15% of 391, not of the original); 376 subtracts 15 instead of 15%; 449.65 increases 391 by a further 15%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Amit's monthly salary is ₹36,000. He saves 15% of it and spends 40% of the rest on rent. How much does he pay as rent each month?

solution.concept: The 40% applies to what is left after saving, not to the whole salary
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹14,400 takes 40% of the whole salary; ₹18,360 is what remains after rent (60% of 30,600); ₹5,400 is the saving, not the rent.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What percentage of 2.5 kg is 375 g?

solution.concept: Convert to the same unit first: 2.5 kg = 2,500 g
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.5% converts 2.5 kg to 25,000 g; 150% converts it to 250 g; 6.67% inverts the ratio (2,500 ÷ 375 = 6.67).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The price of petrol rises by 10% and then by another 10%. A motorist cuts his consumption so that his spending on petrol rises by only 10% overall. By what percentage did he cut his consumption?

solution.concept: Spending = price × consumption; two 10% rises make the price 1.21 times the original
solution.explanation: Price becomes 1.1 × 1.1 = 1.21 times. Spending must be 1.10 times, so consumption = 1.10 ÷ 1.21 = 10/11 of the original. The cut is 1/11 = 9.09%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10% simply matches the second 10% price rise; 11% subtracts the 10% target from the 21% price rise and treats the 11-point gap as the cut; 21% cuts consumption by the whole price rise.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A machine bought for ₹5,00,000 loses 10% of its value every year (on its value at the start of that year). At the end of 2 years it is sold for ₹4,86,000. By what percentage is the sale price above the machine's depreciated value at that time?

solution.concept: Depreciated value after 2 years = 5,00,000 × 0.9²
solution.why_others_wrong: 21.5% depreciates by a flat 20% of the cost (₹4,00,000) instead of compounding; 8% depreciates for only one year (₹4,50,000); 2.8% compares the sale price with the purchase price (a fall of ₹14,000).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A cricket team won 60% of its first 40 matches. How many of its next 20 matches must it win so that it has won 70% of all its matches?

solution.concept: Work with numbers of wins, not percentages: wins needed = 70% of the 60 matches
solution.explanation: Wins so far = 60% of 40 = 24. For 70% of 60 matches it needs 42 wins, so it must win 42 − 24 = 18 of the next 20.
solution.why_others_wrong: 14 wins only 70% of the next 20 matches, which leaves the total at 38/60 = 63.3%; 16 raises the next-20 rate by just 10 points (80%), giving 40/60; 42 is the total number of wins needed, not the further wins.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A number is first increased by x% and the result is then decreased by x%. The final value is 4% less than the original number. What is x?

solution.concept: An increase of x% followed by a decrease of x% gives a net change of −x²/100 %
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 solves x² = 4, dropping the /100; 4 takes the net loss of 4% to be x itself; 16 squares 4 instead of taking the square root of 400.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A transporter's running cost per trip is 60% fuel, 25% maintenance and 15% insurance. The cost of fuel rises by 20%, maintenance cost falls by 8% and insurance cost rises by 10%. By what percentage does the running cost per trip rise?

solution.concept: Weight each component's change by its share of the total cost
solution.explanation: Take the cost as 100: fuel 60 → 72, maintenance 25 → 23, insurance 15 → 16.5. New cost = 72 + 23 + 16.5 = 111.5, a rise of 11.5%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 22% adds the three changes without weighting them (20 − 8 + 10); 7.33% averages the three changes equally; 12% counts only the fuel component (60% of 20%).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: An officer's gross salary has three parts: basic pay is 50% of the gross, house rent allowance (HRA) is 40% of the basic pay, and the rest is a special allowance. The basic pay is raised by 10% (HRA stays at 40% of the new basic) and the special allowance is unchanged. By what percentage does the gross salary rise?

solution.concept: Take the gross as 100 and split it into its parts before applying the rise
solution.explanation: Gross 100: basic 50, HRA 40% of 50 = 20, special 30. New basic = 55 and new HRA = 22, special still 30. New gross = 107, a rise of 7%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10% assumes the whole gross rises by 10%; 5% raises only the basic and forgets that HRA follows it; 4% counts only the HRA's share of the rise (40% of 10).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If A : B = 2 : 3, B : C = 4 : 5 and C : D = 6 : 7, what is A : D?

solution.why_others_wrong: 2 : 7 takes the first term of the first ratio and the last term of the last; 35 : 16 inverts the answer (D : A); 8 : 15 stops at A : C.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If x + 4 is the mean proportional between x and x + 10, what is the value of x?

solution.concept: b is the mean proportional between a and c when b² = ac
solution.explanation: (x + 4)² = x(x + 10) gives x² + 8x + 16 = x² + 10x, so 2x = 16 and x = 8. Check: 12² = 144 = 8 × 18.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.6 expands (x + 4)² as x² + 16, dropping the 8x (16 = 10x); 2⅔ expands it as x² + 4x + 16 (16 = 6x); 12 is x + 4, the mean proportional itself.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: ₹5,500 is divided among A, B and C so that, if ₹100, ₹150 and ₹50 are taken away from their shares respectively, the amounts left are in the ratio 3 : 4 : 6. What is B's share?

solution.concept: Remove the deductions from the total first; share the rest in the ratio; then add each deduction back
solution.explanation: Total deducted = 100 + 150 + 50 = 300, leaving 5,200 in the ratio 3 : 4 : 6. One part = 5,200 ÷ 13 = 400. B's share = 4 × 400 + 150 = ₹1,750.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,600 forgets to add back B's ₹150; ₹1,692.31 divides the whole ₹5,500 in the ratio 3 : 4 : 6; ₹2,450 is C's share (6 × 400 + 50).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In class P the ratio of boys to girls is 3 : 2 and in class Q it is 5 : 7. When the two classes are combined, the numbers of boys and girls are equal. What is the ratio of the number of students in P to the number in Q?

solution.concept: Let P have 5a students (3a boys, 2a girls) and Q have 12b (5b boys, 7b girls); equate total boys and girls
solution.explanation: Boys = 3a + 5b and girls = 2a + 7b. Equal totals give a = 2b. So P : Q = 5a : 12b = 10b : 12b = 5 : 6.
solution.shortcut: Alligation on the boys' share: P has 3/5 = 60% boys, Q has 5/12 ≈ 41.7%, target 50%; the gaps 8.3 and 10 give P : Q = 5 : 6.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 : 5 inverts the answer; 2 : 1 is a : b, the multipliers, not the class sizes; 5 : 12 compares the ratio totals 5 and 12 directly.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The present ages of a mother and her twin sons add up to 55 years. Seven years from now, the mother's age will equal the sum of the twins' ages then. What is the mother's present age?

solution.concept: In 7 years each twin also ages 7 years, so the twins' sum grows by 14
solution.explanation: Let each twin be s years old. In 7 years: M + 7 = 2(s + 7), so M = 2s + 7. Then M + 2s = 4s + 7 = 55, so s = 12 and M = 31.
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 years is the twins' present total (2 × 12); 38 years is the mother's age 7 years from now; 12 years is each twin's age.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Five years ago, the average age of A and B was 30 years. The average present age of B and C is 40 years. Five years from now, the average age of A and C will be 44 years. What is C's present age?

solution.concept: Convert each average into a present-day sum first: add 5 years per person for the past, subtract for the future
solution.why_others_wrong: 34 years is A's age; 54 years ignores the ±10 adjustments (60 and 88 used as present sums); 49 years is C's age five years from now.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Ravi tells his younger cousin Arun: "When I was as old as you are now, you were 6 years old. When you are as old as I am now, I shall be 42." What is Ravi's present age?

solution.concept: The age gap d stays the same: going back d years makes Ravi Arun's age; going forward d years makes Arun Ravi's
solution.explanation: Let the gap be d. d years ago Arun was 6, so Arun = 6 + d. In d years Ravi will be 42, so Ravi = 42 − d. Also Ravi = Arun + d = 6 + 2d. So 42 − d = 6 + 2d, giving d = 12 and Ravi = 30 (Arun = 18).
solution.shortcut: 6, Arun, Ravi, 42 are equally spaced (gap d), so 3d = 42 − 6 = 36.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 years is Arun's age; 24 years takes Ravi's age as the midpoint of 6 and 42 (that is the average of the two ages); 36 years is 42 − 6, three gaps rather than Ravi's age.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average mark of 40 students in a test is 62. On re-checking, 3 marks are added to the score of each of 30 of these students. What is the new average of the class?

solution.concept: The total rises by 30 × 3 = 90 marks; spread this over all 40 students
solution.explanation: Extra marks = 30 × 3 = 90. The average rises by 90 ÷ 40 = 2.25, so the new average is 62 + 2.25 = 64.25.
solution.why_others_wrong: 65 adds 3 to the average, as if all 40 students gained 3; 62.75 adds only 30 marks in all; 62.075 adds just 3 marks to the class total.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of the first nine of ten numbers is 18. The tenth number is 9 more than the average of all ten numbers. What is the tenth number?

solution.concept: Let the average of all ten be m; write the total in two ways
solution.explanation: Total of ten = 10m. It is also 9 × 18 + x = 162 + x, with x = m + 9. So 10m = 171 + m, giving m = 19 and x = 28.
solution.why_others_wrong: 27 adds 9 to the average of the first nine (18) instead of the average of all ten; 19 is the average of all ten; 190 is their total.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of 12 numbers is 40. Each of the first five numbers is increased by 6 and each of the other seven is decreased by 3. What is the new average?

solution.concept: Find the net change in the total and divide by the count
solution.explanation: Change in total = 5 × 6 − 7 × 3 = 30 − 21 = 9. The average rises by 9 ÷ 12 = 0.75, to 40.75.
solution.why_others_wrong: 43 adds 6 − 3 = 3 to the average, ignoring how many numbers change; 39.25 swaps the signs (−30 + 21); 49 adds the whole net change of 9 to the average without dividing by 12.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In a quiz, the scores 10, 20, 30 and 40 were obtained by 3, x, y and 4 participants respectively. There were 20 participants in all and their mean score was 26. What is x?

solution.concept: Two equations: the frequencies add up to 20, and Σ(score × frequency) = 26 × 20
solution.why_others_wrong: 7 is y, the frequency of the score 30; 6.5 splits the 13 missing participants equally; 13 is x + y.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Six different three-digit numbers can be formed using each of the digits 2, 5 and 8 exactly once. What is the average of these six numbers?

solution.concept: Each digit appears in each place (hundreds, tens, units) exactly twice among the six numbers
solution.explanation: In each place the digits 2, 5 and 8 appear twice, so the sum of the six numbers is 2 × (2 + 5 + 8) × 111 = 3,330. Average = 3,330 ÷ 6 = 555.
steps: Each digit occurs twice in each place
solution.why_others_wrong: 3,330 is the sum of the six numbers, not their average; 277.5 divides by 6 twice (15 × 111 ÷ 6); 1,665 divides the sum by 2 instead of 6.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A bank branch has 10 officers with an average monthly salary of ₹50,000, 40 clerks with an average of ₹24,000 and some sub-staff with an average of ₹15,000. The average salary of all the staff is ₹25,000. How many sub-staff are there?

solution.concept: Compare each group with the overall average: the surplus above ₹25,000 must equal the shortfall below it
solution.explanation: Officers are ₹25,000 above the average: surplus 10 × 25,000 = 2,50,000. Clerks are ₹1,000 below: shortfall 40 × 1,000 = 40,000. Net surplus = 2,10,000, which the sub-staff (₹10,000 below the average each) must offset: 2,10,000 ÷ 10,000 = 21.
solution.why_others_wrong: 146 sets the total salary equal to 25,000 × s, forgetting the 50 officers and clerks on the right side; 14 divides the surplus by ₹15,000 (the sub-staff salary) instead of the ₹10,000 shortfall; 42 divides it by ₹5,000.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A dealer buys a mobile phone for ₹12,500 and pays ₹500 for its transport. At what price must he sell it to make a profit of 20% on his total cost?

solution.concept: Total cost includes transport; the profit percentage is applied to the total cost
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹15,000 ignores the transport cost; ₹15,500 adds the transport after taking 20% on the phone alone; ₹2,600 is the profit, not the selling price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A tailor's cost for a shirt is ₹300 for cloth and ₹120 for stitching, plus overheads equal to 5% of these two costs. He sells the shirt for ₹529.20. What is his profit percentage?

solution.concept: Full cost = (cloth + stitching) × 1.05; profit % is on this full cost
solution.explanation: Cloth + stitching = ₹420. Overheads = 5% of 420 = ₹21, so the full cost is ₹441. Profit = 529.20 − 441 = 88.20, which is 88.20 ÷ 441 = 20%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 26% leaves out the overheads (529.20 ÷ 420); 76.4% counts only the cloth as cost; 16.67% takes the profit as a percentage of the selling price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A milk vendor adds 1 litre of water to every 10 litres of milk. His 1-litre measure actually holds only 900 ml. He sells the mixture at the cost price of pure milk per litre. What is his gain percentage?

solution.concept: Find how much pure milk the customer actually gets for the price of 1 litre
solution.explanation: A 'litre' sold is 0.9 litre of mixture, of which 10/11 is milk: 0.9 × 10/11 = 9/11 litre of milk. He is paid for 1 litre, so gain = (1 − 9/11) ÷ 9/11 = 2/9 = 22.22%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% adds the two 10% cheats; 21% compounds 10% and 10% (1.1 × 1.1), but the short measure gives 1/9 more, not 1/10; 11.11% counts only the short measure and ignores the water.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shop sells 400 electric irons a week at a profit of ₹50 each. It cuts the price of an iron by ₹10, and weekly sales rise by 50%. What happens to the shop's weekly profit?

solution.concept: Weekly profit = profit per unit × units sold; the price cut comes straight out of the profit per unit
solution.explanation: Before: 400 × 50 = ₹20,000. After: profit per iron = 50 − 10 = ₹40 and sales = 600, so profit = 600 × 40 = ₹24,000. The rise is 4,000 ÷ 20,000 = 20%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30% subtracts the 20% fall in unit profit from the 50% rise in sales instead of multiplying; 50% counts only the rise in sales; 'falls by 20%' counts only the drop in profit per iron.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: An online seller lists a lamp at ₹1,000. The marketplace keeps a commission of 2% of the listed price, and the seller pays ₹40 for shipping each order. If the lamp costs him ₹750, what is his profit percentage on each sale?

solution.concept: Net receipt = listed price − commission − shipping; profit % is on the cost
solution.why_others_wrong: 33.33% ignores both charges; 30.67% subtracts the commission but forgets the shipping; 28% subtracts the shipping but forgets the commission.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sold an article to B at a loss of 10%. B sold it to C at a profit of x%, and C sold it to D at a profit of x%. D paid 8.9% more than A's cost. What is x?

solution.concept: Multiply the factors: 0.9 × (1 + x/100)² = 1.089
solution.why_others_wrong: 9.45% adds the percentages (−10 + 2x = 8.9) instead of multiplying the factors; 4.36% ignores A's 10% loss ((1 + x/100)² = 1.089); 21% stops at 1.21 and reads it as a single profit.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A manufacturer makes 1,000 table lamps. Each lamp costs ₹150 in materials and labour, and the fixed costs for the batch are ₹60,000. He sells 800 lamps at ₹300 each and clears the rest at a single lower price. At what price must the remaining lamps be sold for his overall profit to be 20% of his total cost?

solution.concept: Total cost includes the fixed cost; target revenue = 1.2 × total cost
solution.explanation: Total cost = 1,000 × 150 + 60,000 = ₹2,10,000. Target revenue = 1.2 × 2,10,000 = ₹2,52,000. The 800 lamps bring in ₹2,40,000, so the other 200 must bring ₹12,000: ₹60 each.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹112.50 takes the profit as 20% of revenue (2,10,000 ÷ 0.8); ₹252 is the target revenue per lamp over all 1,000 lamps; ₹15 divides the shortfall of ₹12,000 by 800 instead of 200.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A cloth dealer buys cloth X at ₹200 per metre and cloth Y at ₹300 per metre, in the ratio 3 : 2 by length. 10% of X and 5% of Y turn out to be damaged and cannot be sold. He sells all the rest at ₹320 per metre. What is his profit percentage?

solution.concept: Take 3 m of X and 2 m of Y; subtract the damaged lengths before computing revenue
solution.why_others_wrong: 33.33% ignores the damage (5 m × 320); 28% compares ₹320 with the simple average cost ₹250, ignoring both the 3 : 2 ratio and the damage; 23.33% applies the average damage rate 7.5% to all 5 m.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shop gives successive discounts of 25% and 20% on a jacket marked ₹4,000. How much does a customer pay?

solution.concept: Apply the second discount to the already reduced price
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,200 adds the discounts (45% off); ₹1,600 is the total discount, not the price paid; ₹3,000 applies only the first discount.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shopping app offers 20% off, subject to a maximum discount of ₹500, and then 5% cashback on the amount paid. What is the effective cost of an item priced at ₹3,000?

solution.concept: 20% of 3,000 = 600 exceeds the cap, so the discount is only ₹500; cashback is on the amount actually paid
solution.explanation: 20% of 3,000 = ₹600, but the cap limits the discount to ₹500, so the buyer pays ₹2,500. Cashback = 5% of 2,500 = ₹125. Effective cost = 2,500 − 125 = ₹2,375.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,280 ignores the cap (2,400 × 0.95); ₹2,500 forgets the cashback; ₹2,400 ignores both the cap and the cashback.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A television marked ₹40,000 is sold at a 12.5% discount. The buyer also hands over his old set, for which the shop allows ₹3,000 off the price; the shop can resell the old set for only ₹1,200. If the new television cost the shop ₹28,000, what is the shop's profit percentage on the deal?

solution.concept: The shop's receipts = cash received + what the old set is really worth to it
solution.explanation: Price after discount = 40,000 × 0.875 = ₹35,000. Cash received = 35,000 − 3,000 = ₹32,000. Adding the old set's real worth, ₹1,200, the shop gets ₹33,200. Profit = 5,200, which is 5,200 ÷ 28,000 = 18.57%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25% values the old set at the full ₹3,000 allowed for it (₹35,000 received); 14.29% treats the old set as worthless (₹32,000); 15.66% takes the profit as a percentage of the ₹33,200 received instead of the cost.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Before a sale, a shop raises the marked price of a cooler by 25% and then advertises 'flat 30% off'. Card buyers get a further 10% off the sale price. Selling to a card buyer, the shop still makes a 26% profit on cost. By what percentage above cost was the original marked price?

solution.concept: Chain the factors: card price = original MP × 1.25 × 0.70 × 0.90
solution.explanation: Card price = MP × 1.25 × 0.7 × 0.9 = 0.7875 MP. This equals 1.26 × cost, so MP = 1.26 ÷ 0.7875 = 1.6 × cost, i.e. 60% above cost.
solution.why_others_wrong: 48.24% adds and subtracts the percentages (1.25 − 0.30 − 0.10 = 0.85); 100% ignores the 25% price rise (0.7 × 0.9 = 0.63); 44% forgets the card discount (0.875).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the simple interest on ₹6,400 at 7.5% per annum for 2 years 8 months?

solution.concept: Convert the period to years: 2 years 8 months = 2 8/12 = 8/3 years
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,344 reads 2 years 8 months as 2.8 years; ₹960 counts only the 2 whole years; ₹7,680 is the amount (principal + interest), not the interest.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Ravi deposits ₹2,000 at the start of every month for 12 months in a recurring deposit that pays 6% per annum simple interest. How much interest has he earned at the end of the 12th month?

solution.concept: The first deposit earns interest for 12 months, the second for 11, …, the last for 1 month
solution.explanation: Interest on ₹2,000 for one month = 2,000 × 6% ÷ 12 = ₹10. The deposits earn for 12 + 11 + … + 1 = 78 months in all, so the interest = 78 × 10 = ₹780.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,440 gives every deposit a full year of interest; ₹720 gives each deposit 6 months on average instead of 6.5; ₹660 counts the first deposit for only 11 months (11 + 10 + … + 1 = 66).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sum doubles itself in 10 years at simple interest. After the first 5 years the rate is raised to 12% per annum. In how many years in all will the sum become three times itself?

solution.concept: Doubling in 10 years means 100% interest in 10 years, i.e. 10% a year; tripling needs 200% interest
solution.explanation: Rate = 100% ÷ 10 = 10%. In the first 5 years the interest is 50% of the sum. The remaining 150% at 12% a year takes 150 ÷ 12 = 12.5 years. Total = 5 + 12.5 = 17.5 years.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 years keeps the rate at 10% throughout; 12.5 years gives only the second phase; 16⅔ years applies 12% from the start (200 ÷ 12).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the compound interest on ₹5,000 for 1½ years at 20% per annum, compounded annually? (For the last half year, interest is at half the annual rate on the amount then due.)

solution.concept: Compound for the full year, then add 10% (half of 20%) for the half year
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,655 compounds half-yearly for 3 periods (5,000 × 1.1³ − 5,000); ₹1,500 is simple interest for 1½ years; ₹1,000 stops after the first year.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: On the same sum, what is the ratio of the compound interest (compounded annually) to the simple interest for 2 years at 10% per annum?

solution.concept: For 2 years, CI = P(1.1² − 1) = 0.21P and SI = 0.20P
solution.why_others_wrong: 11 : 10 compares one year's growth factor 1.1 with 1; 1 : 1 forgets the interest on interest in year 2; 121 : 100 compares the CI amount with the principal.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: ₹20,000 is invested at compound interest, compounded annually, at 5% for the first year, 10% for the second year and 20% for the third year. What is the compound interest for the three years?

solution.concept: Multiply the yearly growth factors: 1.05 × 1.10 × 1.20
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹7,000 adds the rates as simple interest (35%); ₹27,720 is the amount, not the interest; ₹7,100 compounds the first two years but takes the 20% on the original ₹20,000.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How much must be invested now at 10% per annum compound interest (compounded annually) so that ₹13,310 can be withdrawn at the end of 3 years and a further ₹14,641 at the end of 4 years, leaving nothing?

solution.concept: The investment equals the sum of the present values of the two withdrawals
solution.explanation: Present value of 13,310 due in 3 years = 13,310 ÷ 1.1³ = ₹10,000. Present value of 14,641 due in 4 years = 14,641 ÷ 1.1⁴ = ₹10,000. Investment = ₹20,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹21,000 discounts the second withdrawal for only 3 years (14,641 ÷ 1.331 = 11,000); ₹10,000 covers only one withdrawal; ₹27,951 adds the withdrawals without discounting.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A, B and C invest for the same period and share the profit in the ratio 3 : 4 : 5. A invested ₹45,000. What was the total capital of the three partners?

solution.concept: For the same period, profits are in the ratio of capitals, so one part = 45,000 ÷ 3
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹60,000 is B's capital; ₹75,000 is C's capital; ₹1,35,000 multiplies A's capital by 3 instead of dividing by 3 and multiplying by 12.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B invest ₹60,000 and ₹40,000 in a firm for a year. B also lends ₹20,000 to the firm at 10% per annum interest, which is paid before the profit is shared. The year's profit before this interest is ₹32,000, and the rest is shared in the ratio of capitals. How much does B receive in all?

solution.concept: Pay the loan interest first; only the remainder is shared in the ratio 3 : 2; B gets both
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹12,800 shares the whole ₹32,000 and ignores the loan; ₹16,000 treats the loan as capital (60 : 60); ₹12,000 forgets to add the interest B earns on his loan.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A, B and C invest ₹1,50,000, ₹90,000 and ₹60,000 in a firm. B manages it and first takes 10% of the profit as a management fee. Of the remaining profit, one-third is shared equally among the three and the rest in the ratio of their capitals. Out of a profit of ₹1,20,000, how much does B receive in all?

solution.concept: Fee first; then split the remainder into an equal part and a capital-ratio part (capitals 5 : 3 : 2)
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹44,400 shares all of the ₹1,08,000 in the ratio of capitals, ignoring the equal one-third; ₹36,000 gives B 30% of the whole profit with no fee and no equal part; ₹33,600 leaves out B's ₹12,000 from the equal part.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many litres of water must be added to 15 litres of a 12% salt solution to make it a 9% salt solution?

solution.concept: The amount of salt does not change when water is added
solution.explanation: Salt = 12% of 15 = 1.8 litres. In the new solution 1.8 litres must be 9%, so the total is 1.8 ÷ 0.09 = 20 litres. Water to add = 20 − 15 = 5 litres.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 litres is the new total volume, not the water added; 3.75 litres takes the 3-point drop as a fraction of 12 (15 × 3/12); 1.8 litres is the amount of salt.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A farm store has two fertilisers: type X contains 40% nitrogen and type Y contains 16% nitrogen. In what ratio must X and Y be mixed to get a fertiliser with 25% nitrogen?

solution.concept: Alligation: X : Y = (target − Y) : (X − target)
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 : 3 puts the differences the wrong way round; 3 : 8 compares 9 with 40 − 16 = 24, the whole gap; 5 : 2 is just the ratio of the two strengths, 40 : 16.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: 10 litres of a 30% acid solution, 15 litres of a 20% acid solution and 25 litres of a 10% acid solution are mixed. What is the acid concentration of the mixture?

solution.concept: Concentration = total acid ÷ total volume
solution.explanation: Acid = 3 + 3 + 2.5 = 8.5 litres in 50 litres, so the concentration is 8.5 ÷ 50 = 17%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% averages the three strengths without weighting by volume; 23% pairs the volumes with the wrong strengths (25 L of 30%, 10 L of 10%); 8.5% is the litres of acid, not the percentage.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two varieties of tea are mixed. When they are mixed in the ratio 2 : 3 (first : second), the blend costs ₹38 per 100 g; when mixed in the ratio 3 : 2, it costs ₹42 per 100 g. What is the cost of the costlier variety per 100 g?

solution.concept: Write two equations in the two prices: 2a + 3b = 5 × 38 and 3a + 2b = 5 × 42
solution.explanation: 2a + 3b = 190 and 3a + 2b = 210. Adding: 5(a + b) = 400, so a + b = 80. Subtracting: a − b = 20. So a = ₹50 and b = ₹30; the costlier variety costs ₹50 per 100 g.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹30 is the cheaper variety; ₹40 is the average of the two prices (a + b = 80 halved); ₹42 is the price of the second blend, not of either variety.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A jeweller has 30 g of 18-carat gold (18 parts pure gold in 24). How many grams of pure (24-carat) gold must he add to make the whole 22-carat?

solution.concept: Alligation on purity: pure : 18-carat = (22 − 18) : (24 − 22)
solution.explanation: Pure : 18-carat = (22 − 18) : (24 − 22) = 4 : 2 = 2 : 1. With 30 g of 18-carat gold, the pure gold needed is 2 × 30 = 60 g. Check: gold = 22.5 + 60 = 82.5 g in 90 g = 22/24 ✓.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 g reverses the alligation ratio (1 : 2); 30 g assumes equal amounts give the midway purity, which would be 21 carat; 120 g takes the ratio as 4 : 1, forgetting the 24 − 22 = 2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A vessel holds milk and water in the ratio 5 : 3. 16 litres of the mixture are drawn off and replaced with pure milk, and the ratio of milk to water becomes 3 : 1. How many litres did the vessel hold?

solution.concept: Water changes only when mixture is drawn off: after drawing 16 L, water = 3/8 of (V − 16); milk = 5/8 of (V − 16) + 16
solution.explanation: After the replacement, water = 3/8 (V − 16) and milk = 5/8 (V − 16) + 16. Milk = 3 × water gives 5/8 (V − 16) + 16 = 9/8 (V − 16), so 16 = 1/2 (V − 16) and V = 48 litres. Check: 32 L left (20 milk, 12 water) + 16 milk = 36 : 12 = 3 : 1 ✓.
solution.why_others_wrong: 32 litres forgets that the 16 litres drawn off took away milk and water (it uses 5V/8 + 16 = 9V/8); 12 litres lets milk fall but keeps the water at 3V/8; 64 litres divides 16 by 1/4, the final water share.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Printer P prints 1,200 pages in 40 minutes and printer Q prints 1,200 pages in 60 minutes. Working together, how long will they take to print 3,000 pages?

solution.concept: Add the rates in pages per minute, not the times
solution.explanation: P prints 1,200 ÷ 40 = 30 pages a minute and Q prints 1,200 ÷ 60 = 20. Together 50 pages a minute, so 3,000 pages take 3,000 ÷ 50 = 60 minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 125 minutes averages the two times (50 minutes for 1,200 pages) and scales up; 100 minutes uses printer P alone; 24 minutes is the time for 1,200 pages, not 3,000.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A can finish a job alone in 12 days. A and B work on it on alternate days, A on the first day, and the job is finished in exactly 16 days. In how many days can B alone finish it?

solution.concept: In 16 alternate days each person works 8 days
solution.explanation: A works on 8 of the 16 days and does 8/12 = 2/3 of the job. B does the other 1/3 in his 8 days, so B alone needs 8 × 3 = 24 days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 16 days is the time taken together on alternate days; 28 days gives A 9 working days (B then does 1/4 in 7 days); 12 days assumes the two are equally fast.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: 20 men can finish a job in 30 days. After 10 days, 5 of the men leave and 20 women join. A woman does half as much work in a day as a man. In how many days in all is the job finished?

solution.concept: Count work in man-days; convert the women to men (2 women = 1 man)
solution.explanation: Total work = 20 × 30 = 600 man-days. In 10 days, 200 are done, leaving 400. The new team is 15 men + 20 women = 15 + 10 = 25 men's worth, which takes 400 ÷ 25 = 16 days. Total = 10 + 16 = 26 days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 16 days is only the time after the change; 36.67 days ignores the women (400 ÷ 15 = 26.67 days after the change); 21.43 days counts each woman as a full man (35 men).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A, B and C together complete a job and are paid ₹24,000, shared in proportion to the work each did. A and B together did 3/5 of the work, and B and C together did 3/4 of it. What is B's share?

solution.concept: A's part = 1 − (B + C) and C's part = 1 − (A + B); B's part is what remains
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹8,000 splits the money equally; ₹6,000 is A's share (1/4); ₹9,600 is C's share (2/5).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A is 40% more efficient than B and takes 8 days less than B to finish a job. In how many days can they finish it working together?

solution.concept: Time is inversely proportional to efficiency: A's time = B's time ÷ 1.4
solution.explanation: If B takes t days, A takes t/1.4. Then t − t/1.4 = 8, so t × 0.4/1.4 = 8 and t = 28; A takes 20 days. Together: 1/20 + 1/28 = 12/140, so they take 140/12 = 11⅔ days.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7½ days takes A's time as 40% less than B's (0.6t), giving 20 and 12 days; 24 days is the average of the two times; 20 days is A alone.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: One worker alone would take 45 days to finish a job. A contractor starts with one worker on day 1 and adds one more worker of the same efficiency every day (2 on day 2, 3 on day 3, and so on). On which day is the job finished?

solution.concept: Work done by the end of day n = 1 + 2 + … + n worker-days
solution.explanation: The job needs 45 worker-days. By the end of day n, 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2 worker-days are done. n(n + 1)/2 = 45 gives n = 9 (9 × 10 ÷ 2 = 45), so the job ends exactly on day 9.
solution.why_others_wrong: Day 10 solves n(n + 1)/2 ≥ 45 but counts one day too many (55 worker-days by day 10); Day 8 stops at 36 worker-days, 9 short; Day 23 halves 45, as if two workers worked throughout.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A man can finish a job in 12 days, a woman in 18 days and a boy in 36 days. How many boys must join 2 men and 3 women so that the job is finished in 2 days?

solution.concept: In 2 days the team must do half the job each day
solution.explanation: 2 men do 2/12 = 1/6 a day and 3 women do 3/18 = 1/6 a day, together 1/3 a day. To finish in 2 days they need 1/2 a day, so the boys must do 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6 a day. Each boy does 1/36, so 6 boys are needed.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 leaves out the men and women (1/2 ÷ 1/36); 24 aims to finish in one day (1 − 1/3 = 2/3, × 36); 2 treats each boy as doing a man's work (1/6 ÷ 1/12).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B together can finish a job in 12 days, and A alone in 20 days. They work together for 4 days; then A leaves and C joins B, and B and C finish the job in another 6 days. The payment of ₹18,000 is shared in proportion to the work done. What is C's share?

solution.concept: Find B's rate from A + B; C's work is whatever is left after A's and B's contributions
solution.explanation: B's rate = 1/12 − 1/20 = 1/30. In 4 days A and B do 4/12 = 1/3. B then works 6 more days: 6/30 = 1/5. C does the rest: 1 − 1/3 − 1/5 = 7/15. C's share = 7/15 × 18,000 = ₹8,400.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹6,000 splits the money equally among three; ₹3,600 is B's pay for his last 6 days (1/5); ₹12,000 gives C all of the last 2/3 of the job, forgetting B's part in it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Three identical pipes together fill a tank in 8 hours. How long will four such pipes take to fill it?

solution.concept: More pipes, less time: the time varies inversely as the number of pipes
solution.explanation: Work = 3 × 8 = 24 pipe-hours. Four pipes take 24 ÷ 4 = 6 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10⅔ hours treats time as rising with the number of pipes (8 × 4/3); 2 hours divides 8 by 4; 24 hours is the time one pipe alone would take.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Pipe A alone fills a tank in 10 hours. A leak develops that alone would empty the full tank in 30 hours. A second pipe B is opened along with A so that the tank still fills in 10 hours. How long would B alone take to fill the tank?

solution.concept: For the filling time to stay at 10 hours, B must exactly cancel the leak
solution.explanation: A + B − leak must equal A's rate 1/10, so B = leak = 1/30 of the tank per hour. B alone fills it in 30 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 hours sets B equal to A's rate minus the leak (1/10 − 1/30); 10 hours assumes B must match A; 7.5 hours sets B to A's rate plus the leak (1/10 + 1/30).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A tank has two inlet pipes A and B, which fill it in 12 hours and 15 hours, and an outlet pipe C. With all three open, the empty tank fills in 20 hours. If the tank is full and only A and C are open, how long will it take to empty?

solution.concept: Find C's rate from the three-pipe information first
solution.explanation: A + B − C = 1/20, so C = 1/12 + 1/15 − 1/20 = (5 + 4 − 3)/60 = 1/10. With A and C open, the net rate is 1/12 − 1/10 = −1/60, so the full tank empties in 60 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 hours is C alone, ignoring that A keeps filling; 8.57 hours takes C = 1/12 + 1/15 + 1/20 (adding the 1/20 instead of subtracting it); 30 hours uses the three-pipe rate 1/20 as C's rate (1/12 − 1/20).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A cyclist rides 24 km at 12 km/h, rests for 30 minutes, and then rides 36 km at 18 km/h. What is his average speed for the whole trip, including the rest?

solution.concept: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time, and the rest counts as time
solution.explanation: Riding time = 24 ÷ 12 + 36 ÷ 18 = 2 + 2 = 4 hours; with the rest, 4.5 hours. Distance = 60 km. Average speed = 60 ÷ 4.5 = 13⅓ km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 km/h leaves out the rest (60 ÷ 4); 14.4 km/h uses the equal-distance formula 2 × 12 × 18 ÷ 30, but the two distances differ and the rest is ignored; 13.95 km/h reads 30 minutes as 0.3 hour.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A car covers a distance in 3 hours at 40 km/h. At what speed must it travel to cover the same distance in 2 hours 24 minutes?

solution.concept: Distance = 40 × 3 = 120 km; 2 hours 24 minutes = 2.4 hours
solution.explanation: Distance = 120 km. 2 h 24 min = 2 + 24/60 = 2.4 hours. Speed = 120 ÷ 2.4 = 50 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 48 km/h raises the speed by 20% because the time falls by 20%, but speed must rise by 25% (3 ÷ 2.4 = 1.25); 60 km/h uses 2 hours; 53.57 km/h reads 2 hours 24 minutes as 2.24 hours.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B start at the same moment from the two ends of a straight 1 km track and run towards each other at 5 m/s and 3 m/s. Each turns back at once on reaching an end and keeps running. After how many seconds do they meet for the second time?

solution.concept: Between the start and the n-th meeting (head-on), together they cover (2n − 1) lengths of the track
solution.explanation: For the first meeting they cover 1 km together at 8 m/s: 125 s. For the second meeting they cover 3 km together: 3,000 ÷ 8 = 375 s. (A turns at 200 s; B turns at 333⅓ s; they meet 125 m from A's start at 375 s.)
solution.why_others_wrong: 125 seconds is the first meeting; 250 seconds assumes they cover 2 km together, as if they met again after each covering one more length; 500 seconds uses the difference of the speeds (1,000 ÷ 2), as for overtaking.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: For the first half of the journey time, a car runs at 40 km/h. At what speed must it run for the second half of the time so that its average speed for the whole journey is 48 km/h?

solution.concept: When the two parts take equal times, the average speed is the simple average of the two speeds
solution.explanation: With equal times t: distance = 40t + vt and time = 2t, so the average is (40 + v)/2 = 48, giving v = 56 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 60 km/h treats the halves as equal distances (2 × 40 × v ÷ (40 + v) = 48); 64 km/h makes up the 8 km/h shortfall twice (48 + 2 × 8); 44 km/h averages 40 and 48.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: At 9:00 AM two cars start towards each other from towns X and Y, 400 km apart, at 60 km/h and 40 km/h. Each car, on reaching the other town, turns back at once at the same speed. At what time do they meet for the second time?

solution.concept: Up to the n-th head-on meeting the two cars together cover (2n − 1) × 400 km
solution.explanation: First meeting: 400 ÷ 100 = 4 h, at 1:00 PM. Second meeting: together they cover 3 × 400 = 1,200 km, taking 12 hours, so at 9:00 PM. (The faster car turns at Y at 3:40 PM, the slower reaches X at 7:00 PM, and they meet 80 km from X.)
solution.why_others_wrong: 1:00 PM is the first meeting; 5:00 PM assumes they cover only 2 × 400 km together; 7:00 PM is when the slower car reaches X, before the cars have closed the gap.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A train runs at its usual speed for the first 60 km of a journey and then at 4/5 of its usual speed for the rest, arriving 45 minutes late. Had the slowdown begun 30 km later, it would have arrived 36 minutes late. What is the train's usual speed?

solution.concept: At 4/5 of the speed a stretch takes 5/4 of the time, so the delay is 1/4 of its normal time
solution.explanation: The delay on a slowed stretch = 1/4 of its normal time. Moving the slowdown 30 km later cuts the delay by 45 − 36 = 9 minutes, so 30 km at the usual speed takes 4 × 9 = 36 minutes. Usual speed = 30 ÷ 0.6 = 50 km/h. (The slowed stretch is 150 km, so the journey is 210 km.)
steps: Delay = ¼ × normal time of the slowed stretch
30 km cuts the delay by 9 min
solution.why_others_wrong: 40 km/h takes the delay as 1/5 of the normal time (the speed falls by 1/5, but the time rises by 1/4); 62.5 km/h is 5/4 of the usual speed, confusing it with the slowed speed; 200 km/h takes the 9 minutes as the whole travel time of the 30 km.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat's downstream speed is 21 km/h and the stream flows at 3 km/h. How long will the boat take to go 36 km upstream?

solution.concept: Still-water speed = downstream − stream; upstream = still-water − stream
solution.explanation: Still-water speed = 21 − 3 = 18 km/h, so upstream speed = 18 − 3 = 15 km/h. Time = 36 ÷ 15 = 2.4 h = 2 hours 24 minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 hours subtracts the stream only once (36 ÷ 18); 1 hour 43 minutes adds the stream to get the still-water speed (24) and so uses 21 km/h upstream; 2 hours 40 minutes reads 2.4 hours as 2 h 40 min.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat whose speed in still water is 12 km/h takes 1 hour longer to go upstream to a place than to come back downstream. The stream flows at 4 km/h. How far is the place?

solution.concept: Upstream speed 8 km/h, downstream 16 km/h; the difference of the two times is 1 hour
solution.explanation: d/8 − d/16 = 1, so d/16 = 1 and d = 16 km. Check: 16 ÷ 8 = 2 h up and 16 ÷ 16 = 1 h down.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5⅓ km takes 1 hour as the total time for both legs; 24 km uses the still-water speed for the return (d/8 − d/12 = 1); 8 km multiplies the 8 km/h gap between the two speeds by 1 hour.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat takes 3 hours 45 minutes to go 30 km upstream and 2 hours 30 minutes to come back. If its speed in still water is raised by 20% (the stream unchanged), how long will the 30 km upstream trip take?

solution.concept: Find the still-water and stream speeds first; only the still-water speed changes
solution.explanation: Upstream speed = 30 ÷ 3.75 = 8 km/h; downstream = 30 ÷ 2.5 = 12 km/h. Still water = 10 km/h, stream = 2 km/h. New still-water speed = 12 km/h, so upstream = 12 − 2 = 10 km/h and the trip takes 30 ÷ 10 = 3 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 hours 7½ minutes cuts the old time by 1/1.2, as if the upstream speed rose by 20%; 2 hours 30 minutes uses the new still-water speed and ignores the stream; 2 hours 5 minutes raises the downstream speed by 20% (30 ÷ 14.4).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat leaves a jetty at 6:00 AM and goes upstream; its speed in still water is 12 km/h. At 7:30 AM a speedboat (20 km/h in still water) leaves the same jetty to catch it. The stream flows at 4 km/h. At what time does the speedboat catch the boat?

solution.concept: Both move upstream: subtract the stream from each speed; the chase closes at the difference
solution.explanation: Upstream speeds: boat 12 − 4 = 8 km/h, speedboat 20 − 4 = 16 km/h. By 7:30 AM the boat is 8 × 1.5 = 12 km ahead. The gap closes at 16 − 8 = 8 km/h, taking 1.5 hours. So the speedboat catches it at 9:00 AM.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9:45 AM ignores the stream (head start 18 km, closing 8 km/h); 10:30 AM adds the stream as if going downstream (head start 24 km); 8:00 AM adds the two speeds (closing at 24 km/h), as for boats approaching each other.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A train 180 m long passes completely through a 120 m long platform in 20 seconds. What is its speed?

solution.concept: Distance covered = length of train + length of platform; 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h
solution.explanation: Distance = 180 + 120 = 300 m in 20 s, so speed = 15 m/s = 15 × 3.6 = 54 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 21.6 km/h counts only the platform (120 m); 32.4 km/h counts only the train (180 m); 15 km/h forgets to convert 15 m/s to km/h.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A 150 m long train running at 72 km/h passes through a 450 m long tunnel. For how many seconds is the whole train inside the tunnel?

solution.concept: The train is wholly inside from when its rear enters until its front reaches the exit: 450 − 150 m
solution.explanation: Speed = 72 km/h = 20 m/s. The whole train is inside while its front moves from 150 m into the tunnel to the exit, a distance of 450 − 150 = 300 m, which takes 300 ÷ 20 = 15 seconds.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 seconds is the time to pass completely through the tunnel (600 m); 22.5 seconds uses the tunnel length alone; 7.5 seconds is the time for the train to enter (its own length).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A passenger sitting in a train running at 45 km/h notices that a 250 m long train coming from the opposite direction on the parallel track takes 8 seconds to pass him. What is the speed of the other train?

solution.concept: For a passenger (a point), only the other train's length is covered, at the sum of the two speeds
solution.explanation: Relative speed = 250 ÷ 8 = 31.25 m/s = 112.5 km/h. Since the trains move in opposite directions, the other train's speed = 112.5 − 45 = 67.5 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 112.5 km/h is the relative speed, not the train's own speed; 157.5 km/h treats the trains as moving in the same direction (adds 45); 18.75 km/h subtracts 45 km/h (12.5 m/s) from 31.25 m/s and leaves the answer in m/s.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A train passes a 200 m long platform in 25 seconds. The same train passes a 300 m long train coming the other way at 36 km/h in 20 seconds. What is the speed of the first train?

solution.concept: Write both crossings with the unknown length L: L + 200 = 25v and L + 300 = 20(v + 10), v in m/s
solution.explanation: 36 km/h = 10 m/s. From the platform, L = 25v − 200. Against the other train, L + 300 = 20(v + 10), so 25v − 200 + 300 = 20v + 200, giving 5v = 100 and v = 20 m/s = 72 km/h (and L = 300 m).
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 km/h forgets to convert 20 m/s; 108 km/h is the relative speed of the two trains (30 m/s); 18 km/h ignores the first train's own length in the second crossing (300 = 20(v + 10) gives v = 5 m/s).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The circumference of a circular pond is 132 m. What is its area? (Use π = 22/7.)

solution.concept: Find the radius from C = 2πr, then use A = πr²
solution.why_others_wrong: 2,772 m² multiplies the circumference by the radius, forgetting the ½ in A = ½ × C × r; 5,544 m² uses the diameter 42 m as the radius; 66 m² is πr, half the circumference.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A rectangular sheet of paper 44 cm × 18 cm is rolled along its length to form an open cylinder of height 18 cm. What is the volume of the cylinder? (Use π = 22/7.)

solution.concept: Rolling along the length makes the 44 cm side the circumference of the base
solution.explanation: 2πr = 44 gives r = 7 cm. Volume = πr²h = 22/7 × 49 × 18 = 2,772 cm³.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,134 cm³ rolls the other way (18 cm as the circumference, height 44 cm); 11,088 cm³ takes 14 cm, the diameter, as the radius; 792 cm³ is the area of the sheet, i.e. the curved surface in cm².

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A cylinder, a cone and a hemisphere have the same base radius r, and the heights of the cylinder and the cone are also r. What is the ratio of their volumes (cylinder : cone : hemisphere)?

solution.concept: Cylinder πr²h, cone ⅓πr²h, hemisphere ⅔πr³, with h = r
solution.explanation: Cylinder = πr³, cone = ⅓πr³, hemisphere = ⅔πr³. Ratio = 1 : ⅓ : ⅔ = 3 : 1 : 2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 : 1 : 4 uses the volume of a whole sphere (4/3 πr³); 1 : 3 : 2 makes the cone three times the cylinder instead of one-third; 1 : 1 : 1 assumes equal radius and height mean equal volumes.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The area of an equilateral triangle is 36√3 cm². What is the area of the circle inscribed in it?

solution.concept: Side from (√3/4)a² = area; inradius of an equilateral triangle = a/(2√3)
solution.explanation: (√3/4)a² = 36√3 gives a² = 144 and a = 12 cm. Inradius = 12 ÷ (2√3) = 2√3 cm, so the incircle's area = π × (2√3)² = 12π cm².
solution.shortcut: The incircle of an equilateral triangle has area πa²/12.
solution.why_others_wrong: 48π cm² is the circumscribed circle (radius a/√3 = 4√3); 36π cm² takes the radius as half the side (6 cm); 3π cm² uses a/(4√3) = √3 as the radius.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The radius of a sphere is increased by 10%. By how many percentage points does the percentage increase in its volume exceed the percentage increase in its surface area?

solution.concept: Surface area ∝ r² and volume ∝ r³
solution.explanation: Surface area grows by 1.1² − 1 = 21%. Volume grows by 1.1³ − 1 = 33.1%. The difference is 33.1 − 21 = 12.1 percentage points.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 uses simple multiples (30% − 20%) instead of compounding; 33.1 is the rise in volume alone; 21 is the rise in surface area alone.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the product of the two numbers is odd?

solution.concept: A product is odd only when both numbers are odd
solution.explanation: Each die shows an odd number with probability 1/2, so both are odd with probability 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 (9 of the 36 outcomes).
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/2 is the chance that one die is odd; 3/4 is the chance that the product is even; 1/3 counts distinct product values (6 odd values among the 18 possible products) instead of outcomes.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: One card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 cards. What is the probability that it is a black face card or a red ace?

solution.concept: Count the two groups separately; they do not overlap
solution.explanation: Black face cards: J, Q, K of spades and clubs = 6. Red aces: 2. Favourable = 8, so the probability is 8/52 = 2/13.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3/26 counts only the black face cards; 1/26 counts only the red aces; 4/13 counts all 12 face cards and all 4 aces.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A tray of 12 eggs contains 3 rotten ones. Two eggs are picked at random together. What is the probability that at least one of them is rotten?

solution.concept: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none)
solution.explanation: P(neither rotten) = C(9, 2)/C(12, 2) = 36/66 = 6/11. So P(at least one rotten) = 1 − 6/11 = 5/11.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/2 adds 3/12 + 3/12 as if the two picks could not overlap; 6/11 is the probability that neither is rotten; 1/22 is the probability that both are rotten.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two fair dice are rolled and they show different numbers. Given this, what is the probability that the sum of the numbers is 7?

solution.concept: Restrict the sample space to the 30 ordered outcomes with different numbers
solution.explanation: Outcomes with different numbers: 36 − 6 = 30. All 6 outcomes with sum 7 ((1, 6), (2, 5), …, (6, 1)) have different numbers. P = 6/30 = 1/5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/6 ignores the given condition (6/36); 1/10 counts sum-7 pairs unordered (3) but the outcomes ordered (30); 2/5 counts them ordered (6) but the outcomes unordered (15).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A fair coin is tossed 6 times. What is the probability of getting more heads than tails?

solution.concept: More heads than tails in 6 tosses means 4, 5 or 6 heads; count with C(6, k)
solution.shortcut: By symmetry P(more H) = P(more T) = (1 − P(3 heads))/2 = (1 − 20/64)/2 = 11/32.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/2 forgets the ties (3 heads and 3 tails, 20/64); 15/64 counts only exactly 4 heads; 21/32 includes the ties (3 or more heads).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many three-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 if digits may be repeated?

solution.concept: Each of the three places can be filled in 5 ways when repetition is allowed
solution.explanation: Hundreds, tens and units can each take any of the 5 digits: 5 × 5 × 5 = 125.
solution.why_others_wrong: 60 forbids repetition (5 × 4 × 3); 15 adds 5 + 5 + 5 instead of multiplying; 243 is 3⁵, the exponent and base swapped.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many arrangements of the letters of the word DEBIT does the vowel E come before the vowel I (not necessarily next to it)?

solution.concept: In exactly half of all arrangements E comes before I
solution.explanation: DEBIT has 5 different letters, so 5! = 120 arrangements. By symmetry, E is before I in exactly half: 60.
steps: E before I in half of them
solution.why_others_wrong: 120 counts all arrangements; 24 makes E and I a single block 'EI' (adjacent and in order); 48 lets the block be EI or IE, i.e. counts the vowels together.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Three married couples sit around a circular table. In how many ways can they be seated so that each husband sits next to his wife? (Seatings that are rotations of each other are the same.)

solution.concept: Treat each couple as one unit: (3 − 1)! circular arrangements of the units, times 2 for each couple's order
solution.explanation: Three couple-units around a table: (3 − 1)! = 2 ways. Each couple can sit in 2 orders: 2³ = 8. Total = 2 × 8 = 16.
solution.why_others_wrong: 48 arranges the three units in a row (3! × 8), ignoring that rotations are the same; 8 forgets to arrange the units around the table; 120 is (6 − 1)!, all circular seatings with no condition.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many tonnes of fish were landed at Malpe in October 2026? (1 tonne = 1,000 kg)

solution.concept: Total catch = boats × trips per boat × catch per trip
solution.explanation: Malpe: 80 boats × 9 trips × 500 kg = 3,60,000 kg = 360 tonnes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40 tonnes leaves out the trips per boat (80 × 500 kg); 3,600 tonnes divides by 100 instead of 1,000; 4.5 tonnes is one boat's catch for the month (9 × 500 kg).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which harbour landed the largest quantity of fish in October 2026?

solution.concept: Compare boats × trips × catch per trip for every harbour
solution.why_others_wrong: Tuticorin has the largest catch per trip and comes a close second (4,62,000 kg); Veraval makes the most trips (960) but has a smaller catch per trip; Paradip has the most trips per boat but the smallest catch per trip.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage did Kochi's catch exceed Paradip's catch in October 2026 (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Percentage excess = difference ÷ the smaller (base) quantity × 100
solution.why_others_wrong: 26.92% divides the difference by Kochi's catch instead of Paradip's; 66.67% compares only the numbers of boats (150 and 90); 13.68% misplaces the decimal point of 0.3684.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the value of the fish landed at Tuticorin in October 2026?

solution.concept: Value = total catch × price per kg; 1 crore = 1,00,00,000
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1.32 crore leaves out the 7 trips per boat; ₹92.4 crore slips one place in converting to crore; ₹10.30 crore is Kochi's value (4,68,000 × 220), read from the wrong row.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Taking the five harbours together, what was the average catch per trip in October 2026 (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Overall average = total catch ÷ total trips; the harbours have different numbers of trips
solution.why_others_wrong: 490 kg is the simple average of the five catch-per-trip figures; 494.91 kg weights them by the number of boats instead of trips; 3,752.73 kg is the catch per boat, not per trip.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many trucks crossed Plaza 3 on that day?

solution.concept: Truck share = 100% − cars % − buses %
solution.explanation: At Plaza 3 trucks were 100 − 55 − 15 = 30% of 3,600 vehicles: 0.30 × 3,600 = 1,080.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,980 is the number of cars; 540 is the number of buses; 1,200 is the number of trucks at Plaza 1.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the total toll collected at Plaza 2 on that day?

solution.concept: Find the number of each type of vehicle, multiply by its toll and add
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹9.18 lakh charges trucks the bus toll of ₹300; ₹9.324 lakh leaves out the buses; ₹10.38 lakh is Plaza 4's collection.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Taking all four plazas together, what percentage of the vehicles were trucks (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Overall share = total trucks ÷ total vehicles; do not average the four percentages
solution.why_others_wrong: 26.25% is the simple average of the four truck percentages (25, 22, 30, 28), which ignores the different totals; 74.23% is the share of cars and buses; 25.00% divides 5,000 trucks by 20,000, rounding the total up.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: At Plaza 1, the car toll is raised by 10% and, as a result, the number of cars falls by 5%; buses and trucks are unchanged. By what percentage does Plaza 1's total daily collection change (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Only the car revenue changes, by the factor 1.10 × 0.95; weigh that change by the car share of the collection
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.50% is the rise in car revenue alone (1.10 × 0.95), not in the total; 5.00% subtracts 5 from 10; 3.02% applies the 10% rise to the car share of the collection but forgets the 5% fall in cars.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many child tickets were sold from Monday to Saturday?

solution.concept: Add the six child bars
solution.why_others_wrong: 2,235 is the adult total; 3,080 adds adults and children; 615 leaves out Saturday.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: On which day was the total number of tickets sold the lowest?

solution.concept: Add the two bars for each day before comparing
solution.explanation: Totals: Mon 460, Tue 405, Wed 505, Thu 400, Fri 570, Sat 740. Thursday (400) is the lowest.
solution.why_others_wrong: Tuesday has the fewest child tickets and comes second-lowest (405); Monday (460) and Wednesday (505) are higher.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the ferry's ticket revenue on Saturday?

solution.concept: Revenue = adult tickets × ₹60 + child tickets × ₹35
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹44,400 charges every ticket the adult fare; ₹25,900 charges every ticket the child fare; ₹30,600 counts only the adult tickets.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: On Friday, the number of child tickets was what percentage of the number of adult tickets (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: 'A as a percentage of B' = A ÷ B × 100
solution.explanation: Friday: 150 child and 420 adult tickets. 150 ÷ 420 = 35.71%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 26.32% divides by Friday's total (570) instead of the adult tickets; 280.00% divides adults by children; 64.29% is the gap between them as a share of the adult tickets (270 ÷ 420).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the average number of adult tickets sold per day from Monday to Saturday?

solution.concept: Average = adult total ÷ number of days shown (6)
solution.why_others_wrong: 513.33 averages all tickets (3,080 ÷ 6); 319.29 divides by 7, the days in a week, though only six days are shown; 447 divides by 5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage was Saturday's ticket revenue higher than Wednesday's (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Compare revenues, not ticket counts; the two fares differ
solution.why_others_wrong: 46.53% compares the numbers of tickets (740 and 505) instead of revenue; 39.73% compares only the adult tickets; 30.66% divides the increase by Saturday's revenue instead of Wednesday's.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the cost of the willow (blade) in one bat?

solution.concept: Cost of a component = (its angle ÷ 360°) × total cost
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹576 is the labour cost (72°), read from the wrong sector; ₹1,260 multiplies the angle by 10 instead of by ₹8; ₹35 is willow's percentage share (126/360 = 35%), not its cost.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Labour accounts for what percentage of the total cost of a bat?

solution.concept: Percentage share = angle ÷ 360 × 100
solution.why_others_wrong: 72% reads the angle as a percentage; 25% divides by the other 288° instead of the full 360°; 0.2% forgets to multiply the fraction 0.2 by 100.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By how much does the cost of packing and transport exceed the cost of grip and stickers in one bat?

solution.concept: Subtract the angles and convert: ₹8 per degree
solution.explanation: Difference in angle = 36° − 18° = 18°, worth 18 × 8 = ₹144.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹18 gives the difference in degrees, not rupees; ₹288 is the packing cost itself; ₹432 adds the two costs.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The factory sells each bat at 25% above its cost. If the cost of willow rises by 20% while all other costs and the selling price stay the same, what will the profit percentage be (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: New cost = old cost + 20% of the willow cost; profit % is on the new cost
solution.explanation: Selling price = 2,880 × 1.25 = ₹3,600. Willow rises by 20% of 1,008 = ₹201.60, so the cost becomes ₹3,081.60. Profit = 518.40, which is 518.40 ÷ 3,081.60 = 16.82%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18.00% subtracts willow's share of the rise (35% × 20 = 7 points) from 25%, mixing percentages of different bases; 5.00% subtracts the whole 20%; 14.40% takes the profit as a percentage of the selling price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The factory makes 5,000 bats a month, and the overheads are a fixed monthly amount equal to the overhead cost shown per bat times 5,000. If production rises to 6,000 bats a month with every other cost per bat unchanged, what will the cost of one bat be?

solution.concept: A fixed monthly overhead is spread over more bats; only the overhead per bat changes
solution.explanation: Overhead per bat now = 30 × 8 = ₹240, so the monthly overhead = 240 × 5,000 = ₹12,00,000. Over 6,000 bats it is ₹200 per bat. New cost = 2,880 − 240 + 200 = ₹2,840.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,880 keeps the overhead per bat unchanged; ₹2,400 scales the whole cost by 5/6, as if every cost were fixed; ₹2,832 cuts the overhead by one-fifth (to ₹192) instead of one-sixth.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage did the number of Bank Clerk students change from 2025 to 2026?

solution.concept: Convert each year's percentage into a number of students before comparing
solution.why_others_wrong: 16.67% decrease compares the shares (25% against 30%) instead of the numbers; 5% decrease is the fall in share in percentage points; 25% increase is the growth of the whole institute.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: For which exam did the number of students rise by the largest percentage from 2025 to 2026?

solution.concept: Compute the growth rate of each group from the actual numbers
solution.explanation: PO 800 → 1,120 (+40%); Clerk 960 → 1,000 (+4.17%); SSC 640 → 880 (+37.5%); Railways 480 → 520 (+8.33%); Insurance 320 → 480 (+50%). Insurance has the largest percentage rise.
solution.why_others_wrong: Bank PO has the largest rise in numbers (320) but only 40%; SSC rises by 37.5%; Bank Clerk had the most students in 2025 but grew only 4.17%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In 2026 the course fee was ₹18,000 for Bank PO and Bank Clerk, ₹15,000 for SSC and Railways, and ₹12,000 for Insurance. What was the institute's total fee income in 2026?

solution.concept: Fee income = Σ (students in the group × that group's fee)
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹6.6 crore charges every student the average of the five fees (₹16,500); ₹5.232 crore uses the 2025 numbers; ₹7.2 crore charges every student ₹18,000.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the ratio of the number of SSC and Railways students together in 2025 to the number of Bank PO and Insurance students together in 2026?

solution.concept: Convert both sides to numbers of students; the two years have different totals
solution.why_others_wrong: 7 : 8 compares the percentages (35% : 40%) and ignores the different totals; 10 : 7 inverts the ratio; 1 : 1 takes PO and Insurance from 2025 (also 1,120) instead of 2026.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How much diesel did the station sell from January to June 2026?

solution.concept: Add the six diesel values
