solution.why_others_wrong: 571 thousand litres is the petrol total; 1,374 adds petrol and diesel; 677 leaves out January.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In which month was the gap between diesel sales and petrol sales the smallest?

solution.concept: Subtract the two values month by month
solution.explanation: Gaps (thousand litres): Jan 42, Feb 44, Mar 43, Apr 37, May 32, Jun 34. The smallest is in May.
solution.why_others_wrong: June is a close second (34); April's gap is 37; February has the lowest petrol sales but the largest gap (44).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage did petrol sales rise from February to May 2026 (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Percentage rise = (May − February) ÷ February × 100
solution.explanation: February 76, May 118 (thousand litres). Rise = 42 ÷ 76 = 55.26%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 35.59% divides the rise by the May value; 42.00% gives the rise in thousand litres as if it were a percentage; 40.48% measures from January (84) instead of February.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the station's total fuel sales revenue in April 2026?

solution.concept: Revenue = petrol litres × ₹95 + diesel litres × ₹88
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹227.30 lakh swaps the two prices; ₹234.65 lakh charges all 2,47,000 litres the petrol price; ₹217.36 lakh charges them all the diesel price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Over the six months taken together, what percentage of the fuel sold (by volume) was petrol (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Overall share = total petrol ÷ total fuel; do not average the monthly shares
solution.explanation: Petrol = 571 and diesel = 803 thousand litres, so total fuel = 1,374. Petrol share = 571 ÷ 1,374 = 41.56%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 41.39% averages the six monthly petrol shares, which gives every month equal weight; 71.11% divides petrol by diesel instead of by the total; 58.44% is diesel's share.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If diesel sales in July 2026 rise over June by the same percentage as they rose from April to May, how much diesel will be sold in July (thousand litres, correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Growth factor April → May = 150 ÷ 142; apply it to June's 130
solution.explanation: April to May: 142 → 150, a factor of 150/142 (about 5.63% growth). July = 130 × 150/142 = 137.32 thousand litres.
solution.why_others_wrong: 138 adds the same 8 thousand litres instead of the same percentage; 158.45 applies the growth to May's 150 instead of June's 130; 140.40 takes the 8 thousand-litre rise as an 8% rise.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many students from Blue house took part in the meet?

solution.concept: Blue + Green = 320 − Red − Yellow; Blue = Green + 16
solution.explanation: Red = 25% of 320 = 80. Blue + Green = 320 − 80 − 72 = 168. With Blue = Green + 16: 2 × Green + 16 = 168, so Green = 76 and Blue = 92.
solution.why_others_wrong: 76 is Green's number; 84 splits the 168 equally, ignoring the 16; 168 is Blue and Green together.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many girls took part in the meet in all?

solution.concept: Work out the girls house by house
solution.why_others_wrong: 182 is the number of boys; 160 assumes half the participants were girls; 146 takes Green's 42 boys as its girls.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many boys from Red house took part?

solution.concept: Boys = 65% of Red's 80 participants
solution.explanation: Red sent 25% of 320 = 80 students. Girls = 35% of 80 = 28, so boys = 80 − 28 = 52.
solution.why_others_wrong: 28 is the number of Red girls; 65 is the boys' percentage read as a number; 208 takes 65% of all 320 participants instead of Red's 80.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the ratio of the number of girls from Green house to the number of boys from Yellow house?

solution.concept: Green girls = (76 − 8)/2; Yellow boys = (72 + 12)/2
solution.explanation: Green girls = 34 and Yellow boys = 42. Ratio = 34 : 42 = 17 : 21.
solution.why_others_wrong: 21 : 17 inverts the ratio; 17 : 15 uses Yellow's girls (30) instead of its boys; 1 : 1 compares Green's boys (42) with Yellow's boys (42).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage did the number of girls from Blue house exceed the number of girls from Yellow house (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Excess % = difference ÷ Yellow's girls × 100
solution.explanation: Blue girls = 46, Yellow girls = 30. Difference = 16. 16 ÷ 30 = 53.33%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 34.78% divides the difference by Blue's 46; 16.00% gives the difference as a number, not a percentage; 153.33% is Blue's girls as a percentage of Yellow's, not the excess.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many jars of pickle did the group sell over the three days?

solution.concept: Saturday = Friday × 1.5; Sunday = Friday + 5
solution.explanation: Friday 40, Saturday 40 × 1.5 = 60, Sunday 40 + 5 = 45. Total = 145.
solution.why_others_wrong: 100 leaves out Sunday; 165 adds the 5 jars to Saturday's figure instead of Friday's; 300 is the number of papad packets.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the group's sales revenue on Saturday?

solution.concept: Revenue = jars × ₹150 + packets × ₹60, using Saturday's quantities
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹9,000 counts only the pickle; ₹5,610 is Saturday's margin over making costs, not the revenue; ₹13,500 uses Friday's 75 packets of papad.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the group's profit for the three days after making costs and stall rent?

solution.concept: Margin per jar = 150 − 95 = ₹55; per packet = 60 − 38 = ₹22; subtract three days' rent
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹14,575 forgets the stall rent; ₹14,075 charges the rent for only one day; ₹39,750 is the total revenue, not the profit.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By how much should the price of a jar of pickle have been raised, with all quantities and other prices unchanged, for the group's three-day profit (after making costs and rent) to be ₹15,975?

solution.concept: Extra profit needed ÷ number of jars sold
solution.explanation: Actual profit = ₹13,075. Extra needed = 15,975 − 13,075 = ₹2,900. Spread over 145 jars, each must cost ₹20 more.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹6.52 spreads the extra over all 445 items, jars and packets; ₹9.66 forgets the rent and so needs only ₹1,400 extra; ₹48.33 spreads the extra over Saturday's 60 jars only.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the occupancy of the AC 2-tier class?

solution.concept: Occupancy = passengers ÷ seats × 100
solution.explanation: 84 passengers in 96 seats: 84 ÷ 96 = 0.875 = 87.5%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12.5% is the share of seats left empty; 114.29% divides seats by passengers; 84% reads the number of passengers as the percentage.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the fare per passenger in the AC 3-tier class?

solution.concept: Passengers = 90% of 200; fare = revenue ÷ passengers
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,305 divides the revenue by all 200 seats instead of the 180 passengers; ₹261 forgets that revenue is in ₹ thousand; ₹2,900 divides by the occupancy figure 90.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many passengers travelled on this run in all four classes together?

solution.concept: Fill in the missing passenger counts from seats × occupancy
solution.explanation: AC First: 75% of 48 = 36. AC 3-tier: 90% of 200 = 180. With 84 and 432 given, total = 36 + 84 + 180 + 432 = 732.
solution.why_others_wrong: 824 is the number of seats; 696 leaves out AC First; 744 takes AC First as full (48 passengers).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the overall occupancy of the train across the four classes (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Overall occupancy = total passengers ÷ total seats; the classes have very different sizes
solution.explanation: Passengers = 732 and seats = 48 + 96 + 200 + 480 = 824. Occupancy = 732 ÷ 824 = 88.83%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 85.63% averages the four class occupancies (75, 87.5, 90, 90) without weighting; 11.17% is the share of seats left empty; 89.69% leaves out the AC First class (696 ÷ 776).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the population of Chandan?

solution.concept: Population = literates ÷ literacy rate
solution.explanation: 1,360 literates are 68% of the population, so the population = 1,360 ÷ 0.68 = 2,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: 924.8 multiplies 1,360 by 0.68 instead of dividing; 1,795.2 adds 32% of the literates, taking the non-literates as 32% of the literates; 1,360 is the number of literates.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In Amla, what percentage of the literates are female (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Literates = 75% of 2,400; female literates = literates − male literates
solution.why_others_wrong: 33.33% divides by the whole population (2,400); 80.00% compares female with male literates; 55.56% is the male share.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which village has the highest ratio of female literates to male literates?

solution.concept: Fill in the missing male and female figures, then compare female ÷ male
solution.why_others_wrong: Chandan is a close second (0.789); Dhaniya has the highest literacy rate but the lowest female-to-male ratio; Bel has the most literates.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Taking the four villages together, what percentage of the population is literate (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Overall rate = total literates ÷ total population; the villages differ in size
solution.why_others_wrong: 77.00% averages the four literacy rates without weighting; 22.12% is the non-literate share; 80.24% leaves out Chandan, whose population is missing from the table.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The number of multiples of 7 between 100 and 200
Quantity II: The number of perfect squares between 100 and 500

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Count from the first to the last multiple (or root) in the range
solution.explanation: Quantity I: multiples of 7 from 105 = 7 × 15 to 196 = 7 × 28, i.e. 28 − 15 + 1 = 14. Quantity II: squares from 121 = 11² to 484 = 22², i.e. 22 − 11 + 1 = 12. Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I < II' and 'I ≤ II' come from miscounting the ranges, e.g. stopping the multiples of 7 at 189 (13 of them) while counting 10² = 100 and 23² = 529, which lie outside the range, as squares (14).
solution.final_answer: Option A: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Simple interest (₹) on ₹5,000 at 8% per annum for 3 years
Quantity II: Profit (₹) on an article that costs ₹4,000 and is sold at a 32% profit

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: SI = P × R × T/100; profit = cost × profit%
solution.explanation: Quantity I: 5,000 × 8% × 3 = ₹1,200. Quantity II: 32% of 4,000 = ₹1,280. Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I > II' and 'I ≥ II' come from compounding the interest (5,000 × 1.08³ − 5,000 ≈ ₹1,299) or from taking the profit on the selling price.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The length (cm) of the third side of a triangle whose other two sides are 7 cm and 10 cm, if the third side is a whole number of centimetres and is strictly the longest side
Quantity II: 12.5

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Triangle inequality: the third side must be less than 7 + 10 = 17; being the longest, it must exceed 10
solution.explanation: The third side c satisfies 10 < c < 17, so c can be 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 or 16. Some of these are less than 12.5 and some greater, so no single relation holds.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I > II' and 'I ≥ II' consider only the larger possible sides (13 to 16); 'I ≤ II' and 'I < II' consider only 11 and 12.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The number of zeros at the end of 100! (the product 1 × 2 × … × 100)
Quantity II: The number of prime numbers less than 100

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Trailing zeros of n! = ⌊n/5⌋ + ⌊n/25⌋ + …
solution.explanation: Quantity I: ⌊100/5⌋ + ⌊100/25⌋ = 20 + 4 = 24. Quantity II: there are 25 primes below 100 (2, 3, 5, …, 97). Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I > II' and 'I ≥ II' come from counting extra zeros (adding ⌊100/10⌋ = 10 as well, which double-counts the multiples of 10) or from leaving 2 out of the primes (24, which would make I ≥ II).
solution.final_answer: Option B: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The number of arrangements of the letters of the word LOANS that begin with a vowel
Quantity II: The number of ways of choosing 2 members from a group of 10

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Fix the first letter, arrange the rest; C(n, 2) = n(n − 1)/2
solution.explanation: Quantity I: the first letter is O or A (2 ways), and the other 4 letters can be arranged in 4! = 24 ways: 48. Quantity II: C(10, 2) = 45. Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I < II' and 'I ≤ II' come from fixing only one vowel at the start (4! = 24) or from counting ordered pairs for Quantity II (10 × 9 = 90).
solution.final_answer: Option C: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the price of one pen?
I. 3 pens and 2 notebooks together cost ₹110.
II. 2 pens and 3 notebooks together cost ₹115.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are needed

solution.concept: Two unknowns need two independent equations
solution.explanation: I alone has two unknowns (pen and notebook), so many prices fit; so does II alone. Together: 3p + 2n = 110 and 2p + 3n = 115 give p = ₹20 and n = ₹25.
steps: I alone: one equation, two unknowns
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I alone' and 'either' treat a single equation in two unknowns as enough; 'neither' overlooks that the two equations together fix both prices.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both statements I and II together are needed

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the value of the positive integer n?
I. n is a prime number between 20 and 30.
II. n + 2 is also a prime number.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Both statements I and II together are needed
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Statements I and II together are not sufficient

solution.concept: List the candidates allowed by each statement and see whether one value remains
solution.explanation: I alone: n = 23 or 29. II alone: n could be 3, 5, 11, 17, 29, … Together: 23 + 2 = 25 is not prime but 29 + 2 = 31 is, so n = 29.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I alone' forgets that 23 is also a prime between 20 and 30; 'II alone' ignores the infinitely many twin primes; 'neither' misses that only 29 survives both statements.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both statements I and II together are needed

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements. Decide which statements are sufficient to answer it.
Question: What is the speed of the boat in still water?
I. The boat covers 24 km downstream in 2 hours.
II. The speed of the stream is one-fifth of the speed of the boat in still water.
III. The boat covers 24 km upstream in 3 hours.

options.text: Only I and III together are sufficient
Any two of the three statements together are sufficient
All three statements together are necessary
Only I and II together are sufficient

solution.concept: Each statement gives one equation in the boat speed b and stream speed s; any two independent ones fix b
solution.explanation: I: b + s = 12. II: s = b/5. III: b − s = 8. I + II: 6b/5 = 12, b = 10. I + III: b = 10. II + III: 4b/5 = 8, b = 10. Any two statements give b = 10 km/h; no single one does.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Only I and III' overlooks that II can replace either of them; 'all three' is more than needed; 'only I and II' overlooks the other two pairs.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Any two of the three statements together are sufficient

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements. Decide which statements are sufficient to answer it.
Question: What will it cost to paint the four walls of a rectangular room at ₹20 per m² (ignore doors and windows)?
I. The room is 6 m long and 4 m wide.
II. The volume of the room is 72 m³.
III. The floor area of the room is 24 m².

options.text: Only I and II together are sufficient
Only I and III together are sufficient
Any two of the three statements together are sufficient
All three statements together are necessary

solution.concept: Area of four walls = 2h(l + b); all of l, b and h are needed
solution.explanation: I gives l and b but not h. I + II: h = 72 ÷ 24 = 3 m, walls = 2 × 3 × 10 = 60 m², cost ₹1,200. I + III: III repeats l × b = 24, so h is still unknown. II + III: h = 3 m, but l + b is unknown (6 × 4, 8 × 3, 12 × 2 all give 24 m²), so the wall area is not fixed.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Only I and III' has no height; 'any two' wrongly accepts II + III, where the floor's perimeter is not fixed; 'all three' is more than needed, since III adds nothing to I + II.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only I and II together are sufficient

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the average speed of a car for its whole journey from P to R through Q?
I. The car covers the 120 km from P to Q at 60 km/h.
II. The car covers the stretch from Q to R at 40 km/h.

options.text: Both statements I and II together are needed
Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not

solution.concept: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time; the distance QR is needed
solution.explanation: I gives 2 hours for PQ. II gives the speed on QR but not its length. With QR = 40 km the average is 160 ÷ 3 = 53⅓ km/h; with QR = 120 km it is 240 ÷ 5 = 48 km/h. So even both statements together do not fix it.
steps: Different QR lengths give different averages
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Both together' assumes QR is also 120 km (giving 48 km/h); 'I alone' and 'II alone' ignore the other stretch altogether.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Statements I and II together are not sufficient
